body:
This confusion comes up a lot and we have discussed how to resolve it a few times, but we can't come up with anything better than what we have so far. 

You are right that the FPS displayed is currently just basically `1000 / MAX(gpu_time, cpu_time)`. It is intended to show a theoretical FPS based on the content on the screen. This means that it implicitly ignores the cost of things like GDScripts, navigation, audio, physics, etc. Once you actually run your game, the CPU is doing a lot more work than it does in the editor. Similarly, when you are running Godot in the editor, Godot has to run all of the editor functionality (and do things like draw the editor itself), so Godot is doing a lot more work than the performance panel indicates. The performance panel only includes the time it takes to update the scene/Viewport, not the time it takes to do everything in the editor. But by measuring with RTSS you are measuring how fast it is to do everything in the editor. 

In general, the information you want is how fast your game runs. Not how fast the Godot editor + your game runs. So the panel is limited to your game. 

Unfortunately, this isn't well communicated. A lot of other users stumble on the fact that if you have vsync on with a 60hz monitor, your actual game only runs at 60 FPS despite the info screen saying your game is running much faster. 

It is just a coincidence that your running game is taking cpu_time + gpu_time by the way. The GPU time is actually measuring the time it takes the GPU to render a frame. CPUs and GPUs work in parallel, so the frame times shouldn't be added together.

Ahaa, thank you! that clears it up alot. The implication is good, however it is as you said miss-leading for the end user unless they have insight into what it actually displays. If it could be documented, that would be very good for these situations and even better would be having 2 different "Frame Timers" where one would display the editors actual frame times and the other "estimated" scene frame time, as both are very useful for optimizations and overall scene diagnosis.
> 
> It is just a coincidence that your running game is taking cpu_time + gpu_time by the way. The GPU time is actually measuring the time it takes the GPU to render a frame. CPUs and GPUs work in parallel, so the frame times shouldn't be added together.

Another thing that I quickly need to clear up, the CPUs and GPUs should only work in parallel when you have "Rendering Thread Model" set to "Separate", [docs link](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_projectsettings.html#class-projectsettings-property-rendering-driver-threads-thread-model), which is normally is set to safe and if I understand it properly, safe should be single threaded, such that CPU does main thread work and only after calls GPU rendering. 
Which would mean you get the rough FPS from doing 1000/(gpu_time + cpu_time) but only when single threaded. Hence when rendering thread model is set to "Separate" the CPU does main thread work and GPU can render at the same time (the last frame) which means you get the rough FPS from 1000/MAX(gpu_time, cpu_time). Is this the behaviour that Godot takes?

> Another thing that I quickly need to clear up, the CPUs and GPUs should only work in parallel when you have "Rendering Thread Model" set to "Separate", docs link, which is normally is set to safe and if I understand it properly, safe should be single threaded, such that CPU does main thread work and only after calls GPU rendering.

No, that's incorrect. The the GPU and the CPU run at the same time. They are two different devices and always run asynchronously. 

The thread model changes how the CPU side of rendering takes place. That time is always captured by `cpu_time` since it takes place on the CPU. `gpu_time` measures the time it takes the GPU to process rendering commands, not the time it takes the CPU to submit rendering commands to the GPU
